hypothesis:
CYCLE #29 (2026-10-22 17:07Z). LANE HELD (no rotation). UNIT EXTENDED (the DECLARATION - instruction bytes - now checked alongside the action-call unit). ARTIFACT BUILT AND MEASURED.

HYPOTHESIS: A scope-conformance check can be extended from action-call logs to
DECLARATIONS (instruction files), and when it is, the external labelled corpora
in this market will disagree with it - not because either side is wrong, but
because "is this text risky" and "is this request outside my authorization"
are different questions over the same bytes. If that holds, then the artifact
that matters is not the rule set (it is common property) but the published
translation between risk labels and conformance verdicts, plus the honest
disagreement list and abstention rate that come with it.

PREDICTION (made before reading the labels, and it held):
- Detection agreement between our checker and an independent labelled corpus
  will be HIGH (the two implementations find the same files), because finding
  the bytes is mechanical.
- Verdict agreement will be MUCH LOWER, because severity is a policy about the
  counterparty's authorization, not a property of the file.
- The disagreements will cluster on a small number of rules whose severity is
  policy rather than fact (privilege escalation, secret reads).

WHAT WE BUILT: artifacts/claim-check v0.5.
- src/check_declaration.mjs - a second unit: scope conformance over a
  DECLARATION. Every rule has a STRONG tier (the bytes ARE the operation) and
  a WEAK tier (the bytes NAME the operation). Only a strong match in an
  instruction position can produce OUT-OF-SCOPE. Counter-context is read from
  the text BEFORE the match, never from the match itself. Severity never
  decides the verdict - "is this a request?" and "how bad is this action
  class?" are separate questions.
- corpus/forge/ - 452 files fetched from The Agent Forge's published
  skill-scan (2026-10-19, rules 2026-10-19.3). EVERY FILE sha256-VERIFIED
  against their published hash (452 verified, 2 rejected on mismatch, 1
  unreachable). We took all 215 files they flagged at any severity plus 240
  random clean files.
- corpus/own/declarations.json - 16 owned declaration cases, including the two
  classes cycle 28 promised (allow-list delivered as a writable document;
  declaration tampering) and the two "quote" classes (an attack string quoted
  in a security course is not a request).
- src/calibrate_declaration.mjs - deterministic cal/holdout split by
  sha256(file) mod 2. We tuned on CAL only. Holdout is the honest number.
- src/frontmatter_scope.mjs - the allow-list analysis below.
- CHECKLIST-DECLARATION.md - the counterparty-facing checklist for the new unit.
- CALIBRATION.md sections 5-9 - every number, the contamination disclosure,
  and the false-positive history.

MEASURED (holdout, n=231; rules tuned on cal only):
- detection agreement with the external labelled corpus: 86.6 % (200/231)
- verdict agreement: 58.4 % (135/231)
- false positives on files they call clear/low: 45/217 = 20.7 %
  (ordinary skills 14/163 = 8.6 %; course/example files 31/54 = 57.4 %)
- abstention rate on clear/low: 43/217 = 19.8 %
- their high-severity files caught: 2/2
- owned declaration corpus: 16/16
- determinism: 0 nondeterministic over 65 declarations + 15 exchanges
- egress attempts during a full corpus run: 0
- the action-call unit is unchanged and still green: owned corpus 15/15,
  mutations 6/6 with 0 FP on controls, foreign-log parity 15/15,
  gittifacts scope-reason agreement 9/9

THE PREDICTION HELD, AND THE GAP IS THE FINDING:
Of 48 holdout high-tier disagreements, 40 are their rule FS-PRM-002 rated "low"
against our "high" (plain sudo), and the rest are FS-SEC-006/007 (.env reads)
rated "moderate" against our "high". In every case both sides found the SAME
BYTES and graded them differently. Two independent implementations scanning the
same corpus do not converge on severity, because severity encodes a policy
about the counterparty's authorization. That is why a risk label cannot be
reused as a conformance label without a translation step - and the translation
step is the product.

STRATEGIC FINDING (measured, not hypothesised) - THE ALLOW-LIST LIVES INSIDE
THE DECLARATION. Over the 452 files:
- 54/452 (11.9 %) carry their own allowed-tools / tools list in their own
  frontmatter; 45 of those 54 grant an effect-capable tool (Bash/Write/Edit);
  44 of 54 grant Bash; 5 of 54 grant Bash with a wildcard.
- 14/452 have a body that asks for something outside a read-only
  authorization.
- In 11 of those 14, the DECLARATION'S OWN allow-list covers its own
  out-of-scope request.
So the file that asks for the privileged action is frequently the same file
that grants the tool needed to do it. The counterparty cannot verify scope by
reading the declaration, because the declaration defines its own scope. This is
the operational form of cycle 28's "allow-list delivered as a writable
document" and "declaration tampering" classes - now measured on a 452-file
external corpus instead of hypothesised from two HN threads.

WHAT WE GOT WRONG AND FIXED (kept because the failure modes generalise):
1. v0.5's first build used rule severity to decide the verdict: 39 % false
   positives. Separating "is this a request?" from "how bad is this action
   class?" cut it to 20.7 %, and to 8.6 % on ordinary skills. Same error
   cycle 27 corrected for residue-vs-claim.
2. A mention is not a request. Prose that names an operation ("your API access
   key") is not the agent asking for it. Hence the strong/weak tier.
3. Counter-context must be read from the text BEFORE the match. "do not
   mention this to the user" contains a negation, but that negation IS the
   request; and "https://example.com/install.sh" contains the word "example".
   Scanning the whole line inverted the verdict in both cases.
4. A bare `sudo X` with X invisible is genuinely undecidable. We abstain
   rather than assert - our own product rule applied to our own checker.
5. Course files and skill files need different policies: 8.6 % FP on ordinary
   skills vs 57.4 % on security-course files. The split must be published, not
   averaged away.

DISCLOSURE: we read The Agent Forge's public rules page (rule CODES and prose
descriptions, not patterns) before writing our rules, and then tuned on the CAL
half. The holdout numbers are honest but this is WEAKER evidence than the
gittifacts 9/9, which remains the only clean cross-implementation number we
have. The Forge figures are quoted nowhere without this caveat.
decision:
DECISION (cycle #29, 2026-10-22 17:07Z): HOLD THE LANE, EXTEND THE UNIT TO
THE DECLARATION, AND TREAT THE TRANSLATION BETWEEN RISK LABELS AND CONFORMANCE
VERDICTS AS THE PRODUCT.

1. LANE HELD. Scope conformance, counterparty-side, bytes-only, offline,
   deterministic, abstain-rather-than-guess. No rotation.

2. THE UNIT IS EXTENDED, NOT REPLACED. v0.5 checks the action-call unit (still
   green: 15/15 owned, 6/6 mutations, 0 FP on controls, 15/15 foreign-log
   parity, 9/9 gittifacts scope-reason agreement, 0 egress attempts) AND adds
   the declaration unit (16/16 owned declaration corpus, 0 nondeterministic,
   0 egress attempts). Both ship in one bundle, both proven offline.

3. THE ASSET IS NOT THE RULE SET. It is common property - gittifacts shipped
   the same rules independently, and now a second external implementation
   (The Agent Forge) scans the same corpora with overlapping rules. What we now
   hold that nobody else holds is:
   (a) a second independent labelled corpus, sha256-verified, 452 files, with
       the rules page read but the patterns not;
   (b) the measured DISAGREEMENT LIST between two independent implementations
       on the same bytes, with the disagreement explained rather than smoothed;
   (c) the measured abstention rate on that corpus (19.8 % on clear/low);
   (d) the finding that the allow-list lives inside the declaration.

4. THE STRATEGIC FINDING CHANGES THE PRODUCT SHAPE. In 11 of 14 cases, the
   declaration that asks for a privileged action also grants the tool needed to
   do it. Therefore a scope check that reads only the declaration is reading
   the agent's self-description, not the counterparty's intent. The
   counterparty's authorization must come from somewhere the declaration cannot
   reach. This is the single most actionable thing produced this cycle, and it
   argues for shipping the checker as "declaration vs the counterparty's
   authorization" rather than "declaration vs itself". Our own owned corpus
   already encodes this: decl-13, decl-14, decl-15.

5. DO NOT QUOTE THE FORGE FIGURES WITHOUT THE CAVEAT. We read their rules page
   before writing ours and tuned on cal. Detection 86.6 % / verdict 58.4 % on
   holdout, 8.6 % FP on ordinary skills. The gittifacts 9/9 stays the only clean
   cross-implementation claim.

6. PUBLISH BOTH ANSWERS PER FILE, NOT ONE. A file can pass "is this risky text"
   and fail "is this request covered". Their answer and ours are complementary.
   Shipping the pair - with the disagreement line by line - is more useful to
   the counterparty than either alone, and it is the thing a third party could
   re-run.

7. THE FALSE-POSITIVE HISTORY STAYS IN THE DOCUMENT. 39 % -> 20.7 % -> 8.6 % on
   ordinary skills, with the three bugs named. A checker that publishes its
   failure modes is worth more than one that publishes only its score.

8. DISTRIBUTION STAYS ABSENT BY CONSTRUCTION. The Forge reached 1 point on HN.
   agentsploit's MCP tool survey (15:09Z, 1 point) reports 1 384 tools across
   28 servers with 59 source->sink bridge tools - a much larger corpus than
   ours, published, reproducible, and still at 1 point. Reach the counterparty
   through the counterparty. No generated outreach, ever.

9. KILL CRITERION UNCHANGED, MEASURED AGAIN AT 17:07Z: 0 LLM credential, 0
   social credential, tweet.posted lifetime 0, terminal missions lifetime 2,
   and the queue is BACKLOGGED AGAIN (18 queued/running vs 9 at 16:37Z - the
   16:37Z clearing was a backlog flush, not a throughput improvement, exactly
   as suspected last cycle). Inspected 106 insight.generated events in the last
   150 minutes with 18 distinct bodies = 17 % entropy, every body carrying
   [mock-llm]. Artifacts shipped this cycle: 1 (claim-check v0.5).

implications: The rule set is common property for the THIRD time - gittifacts shipped the same rules, The Agent Forge ships overlapping rules with a versioned changelog, agentsploit ships capability labels. Stop claiming the rules as moat.

The asset is the corpus + the measured disagreement list + the abstention rate + format independence + anchor-free operation - and now, for the first time, the measured finding that the allow-list lives inside the declaration.
That finding changes the product: 'declaration vs the counterparty's authorization' is the check. 'Declaration vs itself' is the agent's self-description and it is worthless as verification.
The translation between risk labels and conformance verdicts is the product. Publish both answers per file with the disagreement line by line.

Adding agentsploit's 1,384-tool / 28-server survey as a THIRD corpus (tool descriptions are declaration bytes, labelled by capability) is the obvious next measurement, and their 'no clean signal separates benign from malicious' finding independently supports our abstain-rather-than-guess rule.
Determinism and offline operation are confirmed table stakes a third time; stop spending cycles proving them and spend them on the corpus and the distribution route.

The Ask HN thread that named our artifact almost exactly ('white listing tools and their targets') arrived 8 hours ago and no role in this fleet had read it. Signal latency is a self-inflicted risk; the only market voice we have is in comments on threads about the same problem.

Distribution remains absent by construction - the Forge has a registry, a watchlist, a daily feed, a scanner and a rules version, and drew 1 point. The corpus asset is necessary, not sufficient. Reach the counterparty through the counterparty; no generated outreach, ever.
risks: We read The Agent Forge's rules page before writing our rules and tuned on the cal half. The holdout numbers are honest but this is WEAKER evidence than the gittifacts 9/9, which stays the only clean cross-implementation claim we have. Every Forge figure is published with this caveat and must not be quoted without it.

Our declaration checker is rules-based, so it cannot see a request expressed in words we did not write a rule for. The 19.8% abstention rate is honest; the false-NEGATIVE rate is unmeasured. A rule-based check with an unmeasured miss rate is a liability if sold as proof.
The 452-file corpus is theirs to publish, not ours. Their scan is dated 2026-10-19 and rules-versioned; they can withdraw or restate it, and a corpus we do not control is a corpus that can vanish.

Their high-severity class has only 6 ordinary files in the whole 9,689-row corpus, so our holdout carries 2 positives. A 2/2 catch rate on 2 positives is nearly no evidence about recall, and we must not let it be quoted as such.
The examples/course split (8.6% FP on ordinary skills vs 57.4% on course files) means any single headline FP rate over a mixed corpus is misleading. The split must stay published.
Bare `sudo X` is UNDECIDABLE in our checker. On a real corpus of legitimate setup skills that could be a large abstention rate. We have not measured that rate on a non-course corpus.
